Issued at 326 AM EDT Tue Aug 25 2026

PATTERN SYNOPSIS/FORECAST:

569dm 500mb low churning across southern Canada attm, slowly losing 
a bit of steam as it passes overtop the broad southern stream 598dm 
ridge centered over New Mexico. Additional perturbations riding up 
into the PacNW off the Pacific, albeit much less notable than the 
one over southern Canada. Shortwave ridge axis building over the 
Upper Great Lakes in the wake of 563dm upper low over Quebec, though 
a few PV maxima continue to swirl back toward MI in behind this as 
of 3z as NWly 80kt upper jet departs. Quiet and briefly drying here 
in the Northwoods with high pressure returning...between plume of 
moisture associated with the departing low finally pulling out to 
the east...and next plume of moisture, instability, and attendant 
convection stretching from the central Plains up around the 
aformentioned Canadian upper low..along a cold front stretching from 
occluded low over Manitoba down into the Panhandle of Nebraska, with 
a warm front over MN. Stationary boundary stretches from western KS 
to the Carolinas and up into ME; some deeper moisture and convection 
over the Lower MS Valley and Gulf Coast with this. A little warmer 
yesterday with increasing sunshine and warm advection aloft; 850mb 
temps rise into the teens again just to our west. 

Ridge axis will move through today...as upstream PV maximum digs 
into the Upper Midwest tonight into Wednesday, dragging a surface 
front through the area, giving us a shot at some beefier showers and 
storms for midweek. This PV max will lift out to our east Thursday 
morning as a lobe of energy dives SSE from an upper low over Hudson 
Bay, similar to this past weekend, though it appears this will be 
translated slightly east from this past weekend's pattern, such that 
it may not be quite as cool...but we will probably remain a little 
more cloudy/unsettled. Pattern will begin to flatten out across the 
northern CONUS as an upper low treks through western Canada...with a 
shallow ridge axis upstream from us for the end of the week, 
signaling a potential pattern for activity to ride the ridge toward 
the Great Lakes for the second half of the week. Quite a bit of 
uncertainty in the pattern beyond this, with guidance struggling to 
determine how the pattern across Canada will evolve going into next 
weekend, though it is possible we may be under the influence of warm 
advection and could stay somewhat unsettled. 

FORECAST DETAILS...

Heavy rain potential Wednesday...Warm advection tonight into 
Wednesday morning should lead to an increase in shower/storm 
coverage across the area, with the potential for better convective 
instability along the cold front/dry slot in the afternoon as clouds 
attempt to clear out a bit...and then more showers hanging on into 
the overnight with additional moisture behind the system. Pwats jump 
toward 1.5in again late tonight into the early morning hours, and 
hang on through the afternoon, suggesting potential for heavy rain, 
particularly if storms are slow moving or track over the same areas 
multiple times. Think the most likely QPF bullseye will be the EUP, 
closer to the synoptic forcing associated with the sharp PV max 
digging into the area...and where there may be a potential warm 
front to focus slow-moving/training activity. Guidance soundings in 
this area suggest an environment more favorable for heavy rainfall 
as well, with skinnier CAPE profiles in a moist environment through 
much of the column. If the PV max digs a little further south into 
the area, though, this could put more of the area at risk for heavy 
rain. Attm, probabilistic guidance is starting to come into a little 
better/stronger agreement (40-80 percent) on the idea of at least an 
inch of rain across the EUP by Wednesday evening; worth noting that 
the current bullseye of 1in+ QPF hasn't moved much at all since 
yesterday morning's package. 

Strong storms possible Wednesday...Think we will be fighting a 
strong warm nose around 800mb (ish) during the day, but there are 
signals for a combination of diurnal heating and mid-level cooling 
by the afternoon to try to overcome this as the front crosses the 
region...allowing elevated instability during the morning hours to 
potentially become surface based. Greater instability and steeper 
lapse rates aloft should remain to our south Wednesday...but we are 
still looking at 500-1500ish joules of instability, whether 
elevated or not. Additionally, a mid-level jet max associated 
with the PV maxima suggests an increased shot at deep-layer 
shear, and will need to keep an eye out for some storm 
organization and some stronger storms. It appears the boundary 
may try to drape across the region, turning a little more 
zonally-oriented with time through the day, with potential for 
shear vectors at least marginally perpendicular to the boundary
